newsitem.title: MEXICO: Greenpeace says Texas nuclear dump unsafe for Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace says Texas nuclear dump unsafe for Mexico.

text.p: The environmental group Greenpeace said on Thursday a planned nuclear waste dump in Texas near the border with Mexico is unsafe and poses a health hazard to residents on both sides of the frontier.

The proposed dump would be the country's largest for low-level radioactive waste from nuclear plants, hospitals and industries and be located just outside the town of Sierra Blanca, some 16 miles (26 km) from the Mexican border.

Greenpeace said federal Mexican officials seem to have reversed their earlier opposition to the dump despite recent studies showing the site sits on an earthquake zone and could pollute groundwater used by both Mexico and the United States.

"Radioactivity could leak into the Rio Bravo watershed and affect our drinking water on the Mexican side of the border. That is unacceptable," Alejandro Calvillo, a Greenpeace official in Mexico, told a news conference.

Mexico's National Water Commission and Nuclear Safeguard Commission recently concluded the dump posed no health hazard for Mexico, Calvillo said. But he added both agencies used information from U.S. officials and did no independent study.

Mexico's northern states of Coahuila and Chihuahua oppose the dump, arguing it violates the 1983 La Paz agreement that committed both nations to avoid threatening the environment or health of communities within 60 miles (100 km) of the border.
Local residents have accused U.S. officials of using the mostly Hispanic area as a dumping ground for toxic waste because the impoverished residents have little political clout to oppose the sites.
"It's environmental racism," said Richard Boren, an environmental campaigner in the area.
Environmentalists say Sierra Blanca is already home to one of the world's largest dumps for sewage, receiving more than 200 tonnes of New York City sludge a day.
Sierra Blanca residents are in favor of the new dump, mostly because the town is due to get some $30 million over the next 30 years if the site is set up, according to Boren.

But residents of other nearby towns, including the border city of El Paso, have opposed the dump and are using a series of county public hearings to voice their opposition. El Paso wants to use Sierra Blanca's drinking water in the future.
"The bottom line is people in west Texas and northern Mexico are overwhelmingly against the project," Boren said.
